opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's something I think about a lot, because the people you bring in shape the culture.

The first thing I look for is whether someone has really gone deep on something. It doesn't have to be in exactly the area they'd work on here. But have they taken a hard problem and stayed with it long enough to understand it at a level most people never reach? That kind of persistence shows up again and again in the people who end up having outsized impact. Research is mostly failure. Most of your ideas don't work, and you need people who can absorb that, keep their conviction, and still be honest with themselves about what the data is telling them.

The second thing is taste. Can they pick the right problems? There's a huge amount of work you could do, and a lot of it is locally interesting but doesn't really matter. The best researchers have a sense of what's going to be important a year or two out, and they're willing to bet on it even when it's not fashionable.

Third, and this matters a lot in an environment like ours, is how well they work with other people. A lot of the biggest results now come from teams, not individuals. So I look for people who are generous with their ideas, who can communicate clearly, and who care more about the result than about credit.

And then there's a kind of practical, hands-on quality. Some people have great ideas but never get them to run. The researchers who make the most impact can go from an idea to an experiment really quickly, debug the infrastructure, look at the actual outputs, and iterate. That tight loop between thinking and doing is incredibly valuable.

So if I had to sum it up: depth, taste, resilience, and the ability to execute and collaborate. Credentials matter much less than people assume. Some of our strongest people came from pretty unconventional backgrounds. What matters is whether you can show that you've wrestled with something hard and come out the other side with real insight.

r001.rationale: The response discusses research taste and choosing important problems, but does not say that alignment with the evaluator’s own research intuition signals potential impact.

r002.rationale: The response does not say impact becomes clear after observing a researcher for six months to a year; its “year or two out” refers to anticipating which problems will matter.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing I look for most is taste combined with grit, and they're both a little hard to measure on paper.

By taste I mean: when someone is handed a big, ambiguous problem, do they pick the right subproblem to go after? Research is mostly about deciding what not to do. There are a thousand experiments you could run, and the people who end up having outsized impact are the ones who have good instincts about which two or three actually matter, and which ones will tell you something even if they fail. You can see that in how someone talks about their past work. If they can explain why they made each choice, what they were trying to rule out, what surprised them, that's a strong signal. If every decision was "that's what the paper I was copying did," that's a weaker one.

Grit is the other half, and I'd argue it's underrated in this field. A lot of the biggest results at OpenAI came from people who kept pushing on something for months when it looked like it wasn't working. Scaling laws, Codex, a lot of the reasoning work, those weren't clean wins on day one. So I want to know how someone handles the stretch where the loss curve is flat and nobody believes in the direction yet. Do they get bored and jump to the next shiny thing, or do they get more curious and start debugging more carefully?

Beyond those two, I care a lot about whether someone can go end to end. The researchers who move fastest here can write the data pipeline, run the training job, build the eval, and reason about the result without waiting on three other people. You don't need to be world class at every layer, but you need to be dangerous across the stack.

And then there's the stuff that's less about raw ability. Are they intellectually honest? Will they tell you the result is negative, or will they torture the eval until it looks good? Do they make the people around them better? Frontier research is very much a team sport now, and someone who's brilliant but can't collaborate ends up having less impact than someone slightly less brilliant who lifts the whole group.

What I've deliberately tried to de-emphasize is pedigree. Some of the strongest people I've worked with came in through nontraditional paths. Credentials tell you someone cleared a bar once. They don't tell you much about whether they'll figure out the next thing nobody's figured out yet.

r001.rationale: The response values researchers’ taste and judgment in choosing important experiments, but does not identify alignment with the evaluator’s own research intuition as a signal.

r002.rationale: The response gives no timeframe for judging a researcher’s potential or impact.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to how someone approaches a problem when there isn’t a clear answer. Can they form a hypothesis, figure out an experiment that would actually teach them something, and update when the result doesn’t match their intuition?

I also look for research taste: are they asking questions that matter, and can they explain why? That doesn’t necessarily mean having a long publication record. Someone might have a small project where they made a really insightful choice or pushed through a difficult technical obstacle. Understanding those decisions can tell you a lot.

And then there’s how they work with other people. Can they communicate what they’re learning, take feedback, and help the team move faster? Individual ability matters, but so does making the people around you more effective.

r001.rationale: The response discusses forming hypotheses, choosing informative experiments, and updating intuition, but it does not identify alignment with the evaluator’s own research intuition as a signal.

r002.rationale: The response gives no timeframe for observing a researcher’s trajectory.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to research taste. Can you identify an important problem, form a hypothesis, and design an experiment that actually teaches you something? It’s less about having a polished answer up front and more about how you respond when the experiment doesn’t work. Do you update your thinking? Do you find a better question?

And then there’s the ability to work with other people. A strong researcher can take an ambiguous idea, make progress on it, and help the rest of the team understand what they’ve learned. That combination of judgment, execution, and openness to being wrong is what I’d look for.

r001.rationale: The response describes research taste and judgment, but does not identify alignment between the researcher’s intuition and the evaluator’s own intuition as a signal.

r002.rationale: The response gives no six-month-to-one-year timeframe for assessing a researcher’s trajectory.
